title: What insurance records count
bodyMd:
A historian studying a nineteenth-century port found that the number of insured voyages rose sharply after a new insurance office opened. Earlier accounts had treated this rise as evidence of a sudden expansion in shipping. The historian instead compared insurance ledgers with harbour-entry records, which counted arrivals regardless of whether a ship was insured. Arrivals increased only modestly. The new office had offered cheaper policies and accepted smaller vessels that its predecessor routinely excluded.

This did not make the insurance ledgers useless. Their changing composition revealed how financial services reached previously unrecorded traders. But it altered the question they could answer directly. A record created to administer insurance tracks insured activity, not necessarily all activity. Using it as a measure of shipping requires an assumption about the stability of coverage—an assumption the institutional change had undermined.
